answer.query: What can an employee do if they believe they have been unfairly dismissed?
answer.answer: If an employee believes they have been unfairly dismissed, they may make representations in writing to the Director General to be reinstated in their former employment [1]. These representations can be filed at the office of the Director General nearest to the place of employment from which the employee was dismissed [1].

answer.query: Can a dismissed employee claim for compensation or other related claims when filing a case under Section 20 of the IRA 1967?
answer.answer:
Yes, a dismissed employee can claim for compensation or other related claims when filing a case under Section 20 of the Industrial Relations Act 1967. The compensation may include backwages, but there are limits on the amount [1]. 

If backwages are to be given, they shall not exceed twenty-four months’ backwages from the date of dismissal based on the last-drawn salary of the person who has been dismissed without just cause or excuse [1]. For a probationer, any backwages given shall not exceed twelve months’ backwages from the date of dismissal based on his last-drawn salary [1].

Additionally, if the employee has earned money after dismissal, a percentage of such earnings, to be decided by the Court, shall be deducted from the backwages given [1]. Any relief given shall not include any compensation for loss of future earnings [1]. Also, any relief given shall take into account contributory misconduct of the workman [1].

answer.query: What are the requirements for filing a representation for reinstatement?
answer.answer:
To file a representation for reinstatement, a workman must do so in writing to the Director General, and the representation must be filed at the office of the Director General nearest to the place of employment from which the workman was dismissed [1]. 

The representation must be filed within sixty days of the dismissal [2]. However, if the workman was dismissed with notice, they may file the representation at any time during the period of such notice but not later than sixty days from the expiry of that notice [2].

Additionally, the workman or employer may be represented by certain individuals during the proceedings, such as authorized employees, officers of trade unions, or other persons authorized in writing and with the permission of the Director General, but not by an advocate and solicitor [3].

answer.query: How to obtain cognizance for a Collective Agreement?
answer.answer:
To obtain cognizance for a Collective Agreement, a signed copy of the agreement must be jointly deposited by the parties with the Registrar within one month from the date on which the agreement has been entered into [1]. The Registrar will then bring it to the notice of the Court for its cognizance [1]. 

The Court may, in its discretion, either refuse to take cognizance of the agreement if it does not comply with section 14, or require amendments to parts of the agreement that do not comply with section 14 before taking cognizance [2].

answer.query: What are the implications for a Collective Agreement that has been given cognizance by the Industrial Court?
answer.answer:
A Collective Agreement that has been given cognizance by the Industrial Court is deemed to be an award and is binding on the parties to the agreement, including all members of a trade union of employers and their successors, assignees, or transferees, as well as all workmen employed in the undertaking or part of the undertaking to which the agreement relates [1]. 

If any term of such an award or collective agreement is not complied with, any trade union or person bound by the award or agreement may lodge a complaint with the Court in writing [2].

If any question arises regarding the interpretation of the award or collective agreement, the Minister may refer the question to the Court, or any party bound by the award or agreement may apply to the Court for a decision on the question [3].

Additionally, the Employment Act 1955, Part XII does not apply to any term or condition of service provided for in a collective agreement entered into before the coming into operation of Part XII and taken cognizance of by the Industrial Court, while such collective agreement remains in force [4].

answer.query: With the repeal of section 44A of this act, does it mean that maternity protection no longer applies to all female employees regardless of their wage level?
answer.answer:
The repeal of section 44A of the Employment Act 1955 does not mean that maternity protection no longer applies to all female employees regardless of their wage level. The provisions related to maternity leave and maternity allowance are still covered under other sections of the Act, such as section 37(1) [1], which outlines the entitlements of female employees to maternity leave and allowance. 

Female employees are entitled to maternity leave for an eligible period of not less than ninety-eight consecutive days [1]. They may also be entitled to receive a maternity allowance calculated or prescribed as provided in subsection (2) [1].

The eligibility for maternity allowance depends on the length of employment, as outlined in section 37(2) [2], which requires a female employee to have been employed for a certain period before her confinement. 

Employers who fail to grant maternity leave or pay maternity allowance may commit an offence, as outlined in section 94 [3]. 

Therefore, even with the repeal of section 44A, maternity protection still applies to female employees, though the specific details of eligibility and entitlements are governed by other sections of the Employment Act 1955.

answer.query: Company A practices an 8-hour workday with 6 working days per week. To implement the reduction of working hours from 48 hours per week to 45 hours per week, can Company A reduce the working days to 5 days per week and extend the daily working hours to 9 hours?
answer.answer:
Under Malaysian employment law, an employee cannot be required to work more than eight hours in one day, except under specific conditions outlined in the law [1]. If an employer and employee agree in their contract of service that the number of hours of work on one or more days of the week is less than eight, the limit of eight hours may be exceeded on the remaining days of the week, but no employee shall be required to work for more than nine hours in one day or forty-five hours in one week [1].

If Company A wants to reduce the working hours from 48 hours per week to 45 hours per week, it could potentially reduce the working days to 5 days per week and extend the daily working hours to 9 hours, provided that the total weekly hours do not exceed 45 hours and that no single day exceeds 9 hours [1]. However, this arrangement must be agreed upon in the contract of service between the employer and the employee.

answer.query: If an employer practicing a 6-day workweek reduces the daily working hours from 8 hours to 7.5 hours to meet the 45-hour weekly working requirement, how will the calculation of Ordinary Rate of Pay (ORP) and Hourly Rate of Pay (HRP) for overtime payment purposes be affected?
answer.answer:
If an employer reduces daily working hours from 8 hours to 7.5 hours to meet the 45-hour weekly working requirement, the Ordinary Rate of Pay (ORP) and Hourly Rate of Pay (HRP) for overtime payment purposes will be calculated based on the new normal hours of work [1][2][3]. 

The ORP is calculated by dividing the total wages earned during the preceding wage period by the actual number of days the employee worked during that period, excluding rest days, public holidays, or substituted holidays [2]. This calculation will now be based on the new daily working hours of 7.5 hours, which results in a 45-hour workweek [1][2].

The HRP is derived by dividing the ORP by the normal hours of work, which in this case is 7.5 hours per day [1][2]. Therefore, the HRP will be based on the new normal hours of work, which could affect the amount of overtime pay an employee is entitled to receive [1][2].

answer.query: I attended a job interview for a vacancy at a company but was not successful because I couldn’t speak Mandarin. Does this fall under workplace discrimination?
answer.answer: The situation you described does not necessarily fall under workplace discrimination as defined by the Employment Act 1955. answer.query: What elements can prove that someone is an employee in the absence of a written employment contract?
answer.answer: In the absence of a written employment contract, a person can be presumed to be an employee if their manner of work is subject to the control or direction of another person [1]. Additionally, if their hours of work are subject to the control or direction of another person, this can also indicate an employment relationship [1]. Providing tools, materials, or equipment by another person for the execution of work can further support the presumption that someone is an employee [1]. If the work performed constitutes an integral part of another person’s business, this can also be an element indicating an employment relationship [1]. Similarly, if the work is performed solely for the benefit of another person, this can be another factor in determining that someone is an employee [1]. Lastly, if payment is made to a person in return for work done by them at regular intervals and such payment constitutes the majority of their income, this can also be an element that supports the presumption of employment [1].

answer.query: I got fired an hour before work ended without any warning letter or termination letter. My boss told me not to come to work and that he'll pay me a month's worth of salary later, and asked me to give him a resignation letter. What do I do?
answer.answer:
If you were fired without any warning letter or termination letter, and your employer told you not to come to work and offered to pay you a month's worth of salary later, this may be considered a termination without notice. According to the law, if an employer terminates the contract of service without notice, they must pay the employee their wages earned up to the day before the termination, less any deductions the employer is entitled to make [1]. Additionally, if the termination is due to the employer's breach of contract, the employee may be entitled to an indemnity [1].

If the termination was due to misconduct, the employer may have dismissed you without notice, but they must still pay your wages earned up to the day before the termination [2]. If you were not given proper notice or a termination letter, you may be entitled to compensation for the notice period [3].

In Sabah, if you were terminated without notice, your employer must pay your wages earned up to the day before the termination, less any deductions, not later than the third day after the termination [4]. In Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan, the same rule applies, with the payment due not later than the day of termination [5].

If you were asked to provide a resignation letter, this may be an attempt to avoid providing termination benefits. You should ensure that your employer provides the wages owed to you as per the law [1][4][5].

answer.query: In my offer letter I need to give 1 month notice. But I haven't gotten my salary for 3 months, which led me to quit without notice. Do my employers still need to pay me my 3 months salary, or do I need to pay my employers a month salary as compensation stated in the offer letter?
answer.answer:
If you quit without giving notice, your employer is still required to pay you the wages earned up to the day before your termination, less any deductions they are entitled to make [1][2]. This means your employer must pay you the salary for the three months you worked, less any lawful deductions.

If your employer terminates your contract without notice, they must pay you your wages and any indemnity due, not later than the day of termination [3][4]. However, if you are the one terminating the contract without notice, your employer is still required to pay your wages, but they may deduct from your wages any amount you are liable to pay in lieu of notice, if applicable [5]. However, this source has been amended, and the new rule states that wages must be paid not later than the seventh day after the last day of any wage period [6].

Therefore, your employer should pay you the wages for the three months you worked, and you may not need to pay them a month's salary as compensation, unless your contract specifically states otherwise.

answer.answer: The deadline for wage payment is not later than the seventh day after the last day of any wage period [1]. However, wages for work done on a rest day, gazette public holiday, or overtime should be paid not later than the last day of the next wage period [2]. If an employee's contract of service terminates normally, wages should be paid not later than the day the contract terminates [3]. If an employee terminates the contract without notice, wages should be paid not later than the third day after the termination of the contract [4]. A wage period specified in the contract of service shall not exceed one month [5].

answer.answer: Terms and conditions that are less favourable to the employee do not apply if they conflict with the provisions of the Labour Ordinance (Sabah) or any rules, orders, or other subsidiary legislation made thereunder. answer.answer: An employer can terminate an employee’s contract without notice if the employee has committed misconduct that is inconsistent with the fulfilment of the express or implied conditions of their service, after due inquiry [1]. answer.query: When can maternity leave be taken?
answer.answer:
Maternity leave can be taken starting no earlier than thirty days before the confinement of a female employee and no later than the day immediately following her confinement [1]. However, if a medical officer or a registered medical practitioner appointed by the employer certifies that the female employee is unable to perform her duties due to her advanced state of pregnancy, she may start her maternity leave at any time during a period of fourteen days before her confinement [1].

If a female employee starts her maternity leave earlier than thirty days before her confinement, the days she abstains from work in excess of that period will not be considered maternity leave, and she will not be entitled to any maternity allowance for those days [2].

Additionally, a female employee may, with the consent of her employer, commence work at any time during the eligible period if she has been certified fit to resume work by a registered medical practitioner [3]. The "eligible period" is defined as a period of maternity leave of not less than ninety-eight consecutive days [4].

answer.answer:

answer.query: How many days of annual leave is an employee entitled to?
answer.answer:
An employee is entitled to paid annual leave based on the length of their continuous service with the same employer. If they have been employed for less than two years, they are entitled to eight days of annual leave for every twelve months of service. If they have been employed for two years or more but less than five years, they are entitled to twelve days of annual leave for every twelve months of service. If they have been employed for five years or more, they are entitled to sixteen days of annual leave for every twelve months of service [1]. 

If an employee has not completed twelve months of continuous service with the same employer during the year in which their contract of service terminates, their entitlement to paid annual leave shall be in direct proportion to the number of completed months of service [1]. 

Additionally, any fraction of a day of annual leave calculated which is less than one-half of a day shall be disregarded, and where the fraction of a day is one-half or more it shall be deemed to be one day [1]. 

It is also important to note that if an employee absents themselves from work without the permission of their employer and without reasonable excuse for more than ten per centum of the working days during the twelve months of continuous service in respect of which their entitlement to such leave accrues, they shall not be entitled to such leave [1].

answer.query: What is the new entitlement for sick leave and hospitalisation leave effective from 1 May 2025?
answer.answer:
The new entitlement for sick leave and hospitalisation leave effective from 1 May 2025 is that an employee is entitled to paid sick leave after examination by a registered medical practitioner appointed by the employer or another registered medical practitioner or a medical officer if the employer has not appointed one or if it is not obtainable within a reasonable time or distance [1].

For sick leave where no hospitalization is necessary, the entitlement is fourteen days in the aggregate in each calendar year if the employee has been employed for less than two years, eighteen days if employed for two years or more but less than five years, and twenty-two days if employed for five years or more [1].

For hospitalisation leave, an employee is entitled to sixty days in the aggregate in each calendar year if hospitalisation is necessary, as certified by a registered medical practitioner or medical officer [1].

The total number of days of paid sick leave in a calendar year which an employee is entitled to under this section shall be sixty days in the aggregate [1].

Additionally, an employee is entitled to paid sick leave after examination by a dental surgeon as defined in the Dental Act 1971, and this entitlement is inclusive of the number of days provided for under the previous paragraphs [2].

answer.query: What is the limit for overtime work?
answer.answer:
The limit for overtime work in Sarawak is determined by the average number of hours worked over any period of three weeks, or over any period exceeding three weeks as may be approved by the Director, which should not exceed forty-five hours per week [1][2].

answer.query: How to file a complaint?
answer.answer:
To file a complaint, you can present a written statement of your complaint and the remedy you seek to the Director. This can be done either in writing or by making a personal statement to the Director [1]. 

If the complaint relates to a contravention of specific sections (such as section 4, 5, or 7 of the Industrial Relations Act 1967), it may be lodged in writing to the Director General, detailing all the facts and circumstances of the complaint [2].

If the complaint is about non-compliance with an award or collective agreement, it may be lodged with the Industrial Court in writing by any trade union or person bound by such award or agreement [3].

In Sarawak, if the complaint is about hours of work, the process is governed by the Labour Ordinance (Sarawak), and any dissatisfaction with a decision made by the Director can be appealed in writing to the Minister within thirty days of the decision being communicated [4]. However, this section has been amended, and the current rules should be verified against the latest amendments [5].

If you are dissatisfied with an award made by the Industrial Court, you may appeal to the High Court within fourteen days from the date of receipt of the award [6].

answer.query: What are the penalties for employers who do not pay the minimum wage?
answer.answer:
The penalties for employers who do not pay the minimum wage are not directly specified in the provided sources. However, the sources do mention penalties for failing to pay wages for work done on rest days, holidays, overtime, and sick leave, but these are not explicitly about minimum wage violations. 

If an employer fails to pay wages in accordance with the Ordinance, they are deemed to have broken their contract of service with the employee [1]. Additionally, for failing to pay wages for work done on rest days or holidays, or for overtime, the employer may be ordered by the court to pay the due wages, and this amount can be recovered as if it were a fine [2][3][4].

For other wage-related violations, such as failing to comply with provisions under Chapter IV (other than sections 11 and 14), the penalty was originally a fine not exceeding ten thousand ringgit, but this has been amended to fifty thousand ringgit [5][6]. However, this does not specifically address the issue of not paying the minimum wage.

The Cap. 76 text retrieved here predates that substitution, so where it reads "worker" or "domestic servant" the operative term is now "employee" or "domestic employee". The wording is not rewritten in the source text, so that the user can still verify it against the published Ordinance.

The text held here incorporates amendments only up to 31 July 2006. Act A1754 has been in force since 1 May 2025, so every provision it amends still carries pre-amendment wording in this document. Those sections are marked status: superseded at chunk level and carry an amended_by link to the operative A1754 provision.
